newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr rally stymied by rate uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr rally stymied by rate uncertainty.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept a toe-hold atop 74 cents at the midsession but its position looked exposed as the market fretted over the risk of a rate cut.
The uncertainty has plagued the market for weeks and contributed to the dollar's decline from 78 cents since the Reserve Bank sprang its last official easing on May 23.

Dealers, tired of all the second guessing, hope it will be resolved one way or the other this week with the release of inflation and wages data for Q2. If these are benign as expected the market will price in an imminent cut and the dollar should lurch back toward last week's 18-month at US$0.7310.

A surprise on the upside -- and it would have to be a big one -- could well trigger a vicious short covering rally to 75 cents and a lot further if the market came to believe the year-long easing cycle was finally over.

By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the dollar holding middle ground at US$0.7410/15 having flinched from a US$0.7437 high offshore but still up on Friday's late US$0.7390/95 which itself was a 1/3 cent better than the session before.
The bounce was attributed partly to a natural correction of an oversold condition and partly to caution amongst bears in case the RBA did not in fact ease this week.
Dealers said a star line-up of U.S. investment banks had been dumping the dollar aggressively for the last few weeks and would have their pips squeezed should the cut not come.

The market saw Friday morning as the first real window of opportunity for a policy announcement assuming, as almost all analysts were, consumer price and wages data due Wednesday and Thursday respectively obliged by being well behaved.

If the RBA did ease by 0.5 point to 5.0 percent, again the general assumption although a move 25 basis points either side of that could not be ruled out, it would take official rates below those in the U.S. -- an event almost without precedent.

Such a crossover was not unjustified given Australian inflation had averaged less than that in the U.S. for most of this decade and the upcoming data were expected to show core inflation at a 27-year low here.

However, offshore perceptions of Australia as a high inflation, high yield country were changing at a glacial pace and analysts expected the reality of lower returns from A$ holdings would trigger more selling in the medium term.
In that case, they expected US$0.7280 support to come under sustained attack with a risk of eventually revisiting the US$0.7070 low from 1995.

Were the RBA to remain silent this Friday the dollar should enjoy some short-covering support but the uncertainty would be far from over since many would assume the RBA was just waiting for its next monthly board meeting on August 5.

Should August 6 pass with no move the market would feel safer about assuming the easing cycle was over, although some analysts thought it not inconceivable the bank would wait for final data on wages on August 14 to see the private sector split and any revisions to the preliminary figures.
It was a downward revision to Q1 earnings growth reported on May 22 which led to the last easing a day later.
If all these events came and went with no news the market would have to seriously reappraise its policy assumptions and that could see the dollar escape the four month-old downtrend.
In that event analysts reckoned US$0.7650 was a reasonable target although even then much would depend on whether the real side indicators like employment and retail sales showed a sustained pick up.
Back in the present, the dollar was holding firm at 85.66/76 yen from 85.44/54 late Friday and at 57.3 in trade weighted terms from 57.1.
